description: Evidence base for the question whether the share of leaders suffering from inner conflict varies along the left-right political axis. Main finding: no single study measures both dimensions in one population. Three separate literature strands exist and are recorded here with their own populations, constructs and measurement methods so that the gap between them stays visible instead of being closed by interpolation.

words.name: leader
words.description: Person holding a formal top position in an organisation or in politics; used here as the umbrella term covering the two disjoint populations 'corporate executive' and 'elected politician'

words.name: corporate executive
words.description: CEO, C-level officer or company founder; the population of the occupational-health strand

words.name: elected politician
words.description: Member of a parliament or congress; the population of the Wojcik behavioural strand

words.name: general population
words.description: Non-selected adult survey respondents; the population of the happiness-gap strand

words.name: political orientation
words.description: Position on the left-right (liberal-conservative) axis; in almost all cited studies measured by a single self-report Likert item, which is a known quality limit

words.name: political conservatism
words.description: Right pole of political orientation; the direction in which the correlations below are signed

words.name: inner conflict
words.description: Umbrella concept of the user's question: sustained internal distress. Deliberately NOT treated as one construct here, because the three strands operationalise it differently (see the three words below)

words.name: self-reported subjective well-being
words.description: Life satisfaction or happiness as stated by the person about themselves; the construct of the happiness-gap strand

words.name: behaviourally displayed happiness
words.description: Positive emotional language and genuineness of smiling, coded from text and photographs; the construct of the Wojcik strand

words.name: clinical depression symptoms
words.description: Symptom load consistent with a depressive episode; the construct of the occupational-health strand

words.name: self-enhancement
words.description: Tendency to describe oneself in an unrealistically favourable way; the proposed artefact mechanism linking the first two constructs

words.name: dark triad
words.description: Psychopathy, narcissism and Machiavellianism as subclinical personality traits

words.name: sadism
words.description: Enjoyment of others' suffering; fourth trait of the dark tetrad

words.name: correlation coefficient
words.description: Pearson r between a trait and political conservatism

words.name: percentage point gap
words.description: Difference in the share of respondents giving the top answer category, in percentage points

words.name: prevalence share
words.description: Share of a population showing a condition, in percent

words.name: sample size
words.description: Number of individual respondents or cases

words.name: number of studies
words.description: Count of primary studies entering a meta-analysis

words.name: probability
words.description: Subjective probability assigned to a proposition, used for the assumed values in this file

sources.name: Wojcik 2015
sources.title: Conservatives report, but liberals display, greater happiness
sources.authors: Wojcik, S. P.; Hovasapian, A.; Graham, J.; Motyl, M.; Ditto, P. H.
sources.description: The only study located that measures political orientation and a happiness indicator in the same leader population. Study 1 (N = 1433) shows the self-report advantage of conservatives is fully mediated by self-enhancement. Studies 2-4 (N = 4936) use behavioural measures: the 2013 Congressional Record and the official portrait photographs of all members of the 113th US Congress, plus Twitter and LinkedIn users.

sources.name: Van Hiel 2015 comment
sources.title: Defining the happiness gap
sources.authors: Van Hiel, A.; Roets, A.; Van Assche, J.; Bostyn, D.; De keersmaecker, J.; Haesevoets, T.; Joosten, A.; Stadeus, J.; Onraet, E.
sources.description: Published critique of Wojcik 2015. Recorded here so that the contested status of the behavioural finding is part of the dataset. Author response: doi 10.1126/science.348.6240.1216-b

sources.name: Bartolo 2024
sources.title: Associations between the dark tetrad and political orientation: a systematic review with meta-analysis
sources.description: Volume, article number and year taken from the publisher listing; the DOI was not retrieved in this session and is therefore left empty rather than reconstructed from the usual Elsevier pattern.

sources.name: Okulicz-Kozaryn 2016
sources.title: Are conservatives happier than liberals? Not always and not everywhere
sources.description: Two studies, US time series (N = 40000) and 92 countries (N = 230000). Conservatives are happier only to the extent that conservative ideology prevails in the surrounding socio-cultural context. Author attribution and DOI not verified in this session; cited for the conditionality result, not for exact figures.

sources.name: GSS happiness gap
sources.title: How to understand the well-being gap between liberals and conservatives
sources.description: Opinion journal summarising General Social Survey data. Used only for the size and persistence of the raw gap, which is a widely replicated descriptive figure; not used for any causal claim. The primary source would be the GSS itself.

sources.name: Freeman 2019
sources.title: The prevalence and co-occurrence of psychiatric conditions among entrepreneurs and their families
sources.authors: Freeman, M. A.; Staudenmaier, P. J.; Zisser, M. R.; Andresen, L. A.
sources.description: Best-quality source in the occupational-health strand; entrepreneurs, not incumbent executives. Cited for the direction of the effect only, because neither the DOI nor the exact prevalence figures were retrieved in this session.

sources.name: executive mental health grey literature
sources.title: Aggregated executive mental-health figures (hospital and consultancy publications)
sources.description: Clinic and consultancy publications citing a Journal of Occupational Health Psychology figure and a Harvard Business Review survey at second hand. The primary studies were not located. All values drawn from this source carry low reliability and are marked accordingly.

values.description: Share of respondents answering 'very happy' is about 10 points higher among conservatives than among liberals, in essentially every GSS wave since 1972. Descriptive, uncontrolled.
Study 1, N = 1433. Conservatism predicts higher satisfaction with life; small effect, p < 0.001, robust to demographic controls.
The self-report gap above is fully mediated by self-enhancement, i.e. after accounting for the self-enhancing response style no direct ideology effect on reported well-being remains.

Direction reversal: among members of the 113th US Congress, more liberal members used positive emotional language more often and smiled more intensely and genuinely in their portraits. Effect sign is negative with respect to conservatism. Exact effect sizes per sub-study not extracted here. Contested by Van Hiel 2015 comment.
Combined N of studies 2-4 across politicians, Twitter and LinkedIn users; the congressional sub-sample is a fraction of this.

No association found between political orientation and psychopathy, narcissism or Machiavellianism across 28 primary studies. This closes the most obvious bridging hypothesis between the leadership strand and the ideology strand.
Very weak positive association with conservatism, but derived from only k = 5 samples; the authors themselves flag this as thin.
Studies reporting zero-order correlations between at least one dark tetrad trait and political orientation.

Share of executives reporting symptoms consistent with clinical depression. Attributed at second hand to the Journal of Occupational Health Psychology; primary study not located. No political orientation recorded.
Comparison figure for the general workforce from the same second-hand chain; the two numbers should only be read as a pair, not separately.

Probability that a study exists which measures inner distress and political orientation in one and the same leader population with a clinical or validated distress instrument. Searches across the happiness-gap, dark-tetrad and occupational-health literatures returned none; a low residual probability is kept for non-English or unindexed work.

Probability that the Wojcik direction reversal found in elected politicians would replicate in corporate executives. Held low because the incentive structure for emotional display differs sharply: politicians are photographed and recorded for persuasion, executives are not.

Probability that the self-enhancement artefact accounts for the larger part of the 10-point GSS gap. Wojcik 2015 supports full mediation, but the published comment by Van Hiel and the conditionality result in Okulicz-Kozaryn 2016 both argue that real contextual differences remain.

Probability that leaders carry a higher distress load than the comparable general working population, irrespective of political orientation. The direction is consistent across the grey literature and the better-quality entrepreneur research, but self-selection into leadership and reporting bias are uncontrolled everywhere.

open_questions: The three strands use three different populations and three different operationalisations of inner distress. Any chart placing them on one y-axis is an interpolation, not a measurement.
Almost every cited study measures political orientation with a single self-report item, which caps the achievable resolution on the x-axis.
The entire evidence base is US-centred except Okulicz-Kozaryn 2016, whose central result is precisely that the effect does not generalise across contexts.
Behaviourally displayed happiness is a proxy for inner state, not a measure of it; a person can smile genuinely in a portrait and still be in sustained inner conflict.
